wicked, deal with silence
Answer the cruel with silence, and their words return upon themselves; peace is the only victory.
doha idea: the best answer to a fool is silence
Compose a doha that teaches that the wise do not waste words on the wicked, because every argument gives them more to twist, and silence leaves them with nothing to attack and nothing to win.
I stopped replying to my cousin's insulting messages three months ago, and the insults have dried up by themselves; I'd like a doha out of that experience.
heron, elephant, wicked
The heron's stillness hides a hunger, the elephant's strength hides a rage; beware the wicked who wear both.

Make me a doha that warns the wise about the ruthless who show quiet cunning like the heron and brute force like the elephant, and who destroy others without caring, so one should stay far from their path.
doha plz: wicked folks can be calm like a heron then trample like an elephant, don't be fooled
A man in our area looks as quiet as a heron and as strong as an elephant, yet he uses both for plotting and trampling; write a doha on how to deal with such wicked men.
The false pearl gleams like the true, but one touch shows the glass; so, too, the wicked, dressed in virtue.
Write a doha saying that the cruel often resemble a fake pearl, shining like truth while having no depth, and only a wise eye and a little patience will expose their true worth before it is too late.
doha pls: a wicked man is like a pearl made of glass, shiny outside but fake, so don't trust shiny people
false pearl, wicked
I bought a pearl necklace from a smooth-talking seller who swore it was genuine, but it was glass, and he laughed when I came back; please write a doha about people like that.
A distant relative shoots spiteful remarks at me every wedding, and I've decided to stop attending his events; please write a doha about the arrows of such people.
The cruel word is a silent arrow that wounds from afar; bless the one who walks beyond its range.
doha pls: some people shoot arrows with their words, best to stay out of range
Compose a doha about the cruel person whose words are like arrows, shot to hurt and not to heal, saying that the wise withdraw from his range rather than try to catch every arrow.
arrow, cruel words
deal with wicked, calmly

Can you make a doha saying that the wise person should not take revenge on the malicious or sink to their level, because calm and honest living is the strongest answer and the best way to expose their lies.
When my neighbour tried to spread rumours about my family, we ignored him and carried on; now no one believes him anymore, and I'd love a doha out of this.
doha idea: don't take revenge on the wicked, just move on, it hurts them more
Meet not malice with wrath; let calm be your strength, and their schemes will fail of themselves.
musk deer, hunted goodness

Compose a doha explaining that the evil often target the good precisely because they carry a fragrance of honesty that the ruthless cannot stand, and that the virtuous must remain wise, alert, and unbowed.
doha pls: a musk deer's fragrance gets it hunted, and the good get targeted by wicked people just for being good
The musk deer is hunted for its fragrance; so the virtuous are hunted by the wicked for their goodness.
My honest colleague gets bullied for refusing to join the others' schemes, like a musk deer hunted for its scent, and I'd like a doha for him.
The greedy are never full; whatever you give, their hands remain open and their wants remain endless.
wicked, endless greed
doha pls about greedy people who never get enough, how to deal with them
I kept giving my cousin money whenever he asked, and each time he asked for more with a new excuse; I finally stopped, and I would like a doha on this lesson.
Write a doha saying that the cruel and greedy can never be satisfied by any amount of wealth or favour, and so the wise stop feeding their hunger and use their means for the honest and the needy.
Beware, O traveller, the cup of milk offered by a stranger; the wicked sweeten their snare with kindness.
doha pls: a traveler shouldn't accept milk from a stranger, wicked people drug it, stay alert
The salesman on the train offered milk and food to the traveler next to me, and the poor man woke up robbed; I want a doha about wicked folk who disguise themselves as kind strangers.
Pen a doha for the traveler warning that the vile often come offering milk and food with a smile, and the careful man accepts nothing from a stranger whose purpose he does not know.
milk, traveler, trap
The touchstone tests the metal; the yogi tests the heart; blessed is the one who sees the wicked behind a smile.
touchstone, yogi, wicked
Our village yogi has an eye that, like a touchstone, sees through the fake and the cheat in a single glance, and the cheats fear him; please write a doha about this.

Write a doha that says a yogi's wisdom works like a touchstone, telling the pure from the false in a moment, and the wise person trains his eye to see the nature of the malicious before he lets them close.
doha pls: the touchstone shows what is real and a yogi can see real from fake in people, so be like that and avoid wicked folks
The seed of malice grows even in the shadow of kindness; the wicked can bear no good thing near them.
The seed of rivalry my cousin planted in our family has grown into a shadow over all of us; I would love a doha about how to avoid such wicked people.
Compose a doha showing that the evil person's seed of malice sprouts quickly and casts a dark shadow over all who stand near, so the wise plant themselves far from that shadow.
doha pls: the seed of hate grows a dark shadow of pain, avoid the ruthless person's shadow
seed, shadow, malice
doha plz: a pot of water seems full but a wicked person drains the pot when you're not looking
The chakor in me wanted to trust my business partner, but he kept draining the pot of water that was our shared savings, and I woke too late; write a doha about it.

I want a doha for those trusting by nature, like the chakor, saying that the cruel will take advantage of their faith and drain their resources like a cracked pot of water, so trust should be earned with time.
chakor, pot of water, wicked
The chakor gazes at the distant sky, trusting what it hopes for; the pot of water cracks, and the wicked take what was poured.

Compose a doha that says the malicious, like a tall date palm, are lofty but useless to the weary, giving neither shade nor fruit close at hand, and that a swan-like wise person should not expect help from them.
Tall as the date palm, yet it gives no shade to the swan; so the vile, though great, shelter no one.
swan, date palm, wicked
My cousin is rich and powerful like a tall date palm, and yet when the family needed him he did not even answer calls; I wish to write a doha about relying on wicked people.
doha pls: a swan sits under the date palm but the date palm gives no shade for the wicked, no help from them either
doha pls about fake yogis who rob the faithful, how to stay safe
The fake yogi in our neighbourhood hypnotised half the village and took their savings; I'd like a doha for those who trust false holy men and how to deal with him.
The wicked wear saffron as others wear armour; beneath it, the same hunger.
fake yogi, wicked
Write a doha that warns people that a false yogi can be the most dangerous of the evil, because he borrows holy words to hide his greed, so one must test a holy man by his deeds.
I'd like a doha showing that the ruthless person, like a moth drawn to a glare, is pulled by his own anger and malice into a self-made ruin, and that the wise only need to stay away.
I watched my cruel neighbour fall into debt and illness after years of tormenting others, like a moth drawn to its own ruin; please write a doha.
The moth circles the glare he cannot resist; the cruel circle spite till they burn in it.
doha pls: a moth dies chasing the glare because it can't stop, the wicked also destroy themselves by their own spite
moth, wicked spite
doha: wicked people are like the sun at noon, you can't look at them or get close, just stay in the shade
sun, cruel power
That boss of mine shines like the sun in front of the owners and burns everyone below him; I'd love a doha on how to handle such a person.
The wicked are as the noonday sun, scorching those below; keep away and walk in shade.
Write a doha which says the vile person in power is like the midday sun that scorches all who live near it, and the wise stay out of his path and under the cover of their own quiet work.
The wicked are like the leaf that floats on the stream, joining whichever way the water goes; no loyalty is theirs.
leaf, wicked, stay clear
Write a doha that says the malicious have no fixed loyalty and, like a leaf that is tossed here and there, side with whoever is powerful, and so the wise do not lean on them in hard times.
doha pls: wicked people follow whoever is winning, like leaves in the wind, never rely on them
A man I know changes his loyalty as often as a leaf changes direction in the breeze, and he betrayed us when we were weakest; I need a doha about such people.
sand, net, wicked
doha plz: wicked people build on sand and set nets for others, but their own fortunes sink
Give me a doha that says the evil cast nets for others but build their own fortune on the sand of lies, so they do not last long, and the wise only need to avoid their nets with patience.
The net of the wicked is spread on shifting sand, and the catch is only their own ruin.
A man in our town cast a net of false cases around his rivals and built his empire on sand, but it all collapsed last year; I want a doha.
The cleric wears white cotton, but the whiteness stops at the skin; keep away from the wicked who wear piety as a robe.
A cleric in our town wears the finest cotton robes, and speaks of piety, but cheats the orphans' fund; I'd like a doha on dealing with such men of religion.
cleric, cotton, hypocrite
Write a doha that says the ruthless sometimes hide behind spotless cotton robes and holy speeches of a cleric, and the wise judge a man by his deeds and not by how clean his garments are.
doha pls: a clean cotton robe doesn't make a clean cleric, some are wicked, be careful
After I stopped meeting my cruel relatives, my life became so calm that I wonder why I tolerated them for so long; could you write a doha?
Keep away from the wicked as you would from sickness; sweet are the days that pass without them.
avoid evil company
doha pls: wicked people should be avoided like a plague
Write a doha saying that the cruel bring trouble wherever they go, and a wise man arranges his life so that he sees them seldom, speaks to them briefly, and trusts them never.
washerman, wicked heart
doha pls: a washerman can wash dirty garments but not a dirty heart, evil people stay dirty
The washerman in our street can clean any stain but he said even he can't clean my cruel uncle's reputation; please write a doha about the wicked.
Please craft a couplet that says the washerman may remove the dirt from a person's garments but cannot clean the dirt of malice from a heart, so a wise man avoids those whose stains are inward.
The washerman cleanses the garment at the water's edge, yet no washing can cleanse an evil mind.
wicked, calm response
The cruel mock the humble now, but time will mock them in return; be calm and keep your path.
doha pls: how to keep your cool around mean people
Write a doha that teaches patience in the face of the vile, saying that the humble should not be provoked into anger by their taunts, because anger is the reward that the malicious seek.
My neighbours made fun of our small dwelling for years, and I never answered back; now they come to us asking for help, and I want a doha about this.
Leave the cruel behind, and the heart grows lighter, the day grows kinder, and peace returns.

Compose a doha that says the greatest freedom comes from walking away from the ruthless, those who drain our patience, steal our peace and give nothing back, and that this distance is no cruelty but wisdom.
doha pls: leaving wicked people is the best gift you give yourself
leave wicked ones
I finally walked away from a friend who had lied and cheated for years, and my life became lighter; a doha for those who stay too long with the wicked, please.
Make me a doha that says the vile bark at the noble like dogs at the moon, and like a drop of sour in milk they spoil what is pure, so the noble walk on in calm and keep distance.
The moon-like calm of my teacher never broke even when a wicked rival tried to spoil his name like a drop of sour on milk; please write a doha about him.
The moon keeps her cool light though the cur may howl; the cruel bark, the noble walk on.
doha pls: the moon stays cool in the sky even though dogs bark at it, and milk is spoiled by one drop of the wicked, ignore them
moon, milk, wicked
Ram, Rahim, house, one-string lute
doha: Ram and Rahim live in one house, sing it on a one-string lute
Our street singer plays a one-string lute for Hindu and Muslim families alike, and the neighbours sit in one house to hear him, until a fight about names started. Doha for him?
Two brothers quarrel over whether to call the Lord Ram or Rahim, but the Lord lives in one house with both names, and the one-string lute sings the same single note for Hindu and Muslim alike.
One house holds both names of the Beloved, and the one-string lute sings them in a single breath.
In our village the Hindu cotton picker and the Muslim weaver work side by side, but at festival time they fight over whose God is truer, though even the fish in the pond don't care. A doha?
Cotton is picked by Hindu hands and spun by Muslim hands, and a fish in the pond feeds both; so why do the people who share the cloth quarrel over whether the Lord is Ram or Rahim?
Ram, Rahim, cotton, fish
doha about Hindu and Muslim fighting while a fish swims in the same water and cotton clothes both
The fish swims in one water, the cotton clothes both faiths; whose Lord then is only half the Lord?
A doha for those who spread the net of religious hatred over the land, Hindu against Muslim, when the same Lord named Ram by one and Rahim by the other is calling to all of them.

Last week there was a riot over a religious procession in our city, and a net of rumours on phones made it worse. Hindu and Muslim neighbours who had been friends for years stopped speaking. Doha for them?
net, Ram and Rahim
doha: net of religion trapping Hindus and Muslims who worship the same God
The net of names is cast over the people; Ram and Rahim, the Lord is one.
doha: mountain trek, Hindu and Muslim trekkers praying together while a peacock calls
Mount a mountain and see the peacock dance for all; the sky does not ask whether you say Ram or Rahim.
We trekked up a mountain with Hindu and Muslim friends, and at the top we all said our own prayers in the same silence while a peacock called. Could you write a doha?
mountain, peacock, Ram and Rahim
Write about the mountain peak where Hindu and Muslim pilgrims climb by different paths to reach the same summit, and the peacock dances for all of them without asking what name they call the Lord.
doha pls: in the end, forest, shroud, Hindu and Muslim both are same
shroud, forest, Ram and Rahim
In the forest all branches rustle in one wind; in the shroud all are one, whether Ram or Rahim.
In our village, there is a forest where Hindus and Muslims both come to bury or burn their dead, and the same white shroud is used. I wonder what the elders would say. Doha?
Both Hindu and Muslim, when they die, are wrapped in a simple shroud and left to the same earth or the same forest, so why do the living quarrel about whether Ram or Rahim is Lord?
doha about oil press and cloth sheet being used by both Hindus and Muslims, so why fight
The oil press in our town is run by a Muslim and its oil lights Hindu homes, the cloth sheet woven by Hindus covers Muslim prayer floors, so why fight over names when the Lord is one?
The oil press is turned for all, the cloth sheet spread for all, and Ram and Rahim are one.
The oil press owner in our lane is Muslim and the cloth sheet seller is Hindu, and they fought over a religious slogan last week though they run the same trade. Doha idea?
oil press, cloth sheet, Ram-Rahim
Why do you fight over names, Hindu and Muslim, when the One you pray to is not divided by your quarrels, and Ram and Rahim are only two words for the same unnameable Lord?
doha: Ram and Rahim are the same, stop fighting over religion
Ram, Rahim, same Lord
My best friend is Muslim and I am Hindu, and last week his relatives and mine nearly came to blows over a religious issue. We just stood there looking at each other. A doha?
Ram and Rahim, two words for a single Beloved; why do the lovers fight?
sand, mirror, Hindu and Muslim
The grains of sand in the desert are of many shapes, and the mirror shows the face of Hindu and Muslim alike; the Lord who made them is not the possession of any one faith or name.
Sand of many grains, one desert; mirror of many faces, one seeing.
I gave my Hindu friend and my Muslim friend the same mirror to look into, and they laughed at what they saw, the same human face. It reminded me of sand slipping through fingers. A doha?
doha: sand and a mirror, they treat Hindu and Muslim the same, so does God
A verse that tells the Hindu who bows toward the east and the Muslim who bows toward the west that the Lord whom both seek is neither east nor west, but in the heart of each.
In my city the Hindu quarter and the Muslim quarter face each other across a road, and the kids from each side play cricket together while the parents glare. A doha?
East or west, whichever way you bow, the Beloved is waiting where you stand.
doha: hindus and muslims worship differently but the god is the same
East, West, same Lord
The tortoise with its shell of faith and the warrior with his sword of pride both come to the same Lord, whether they call Him Ram or Rahim.
My grandfather, a soldier who kept a sword on the wall, said a Hindu soldier and a Muslim soldier die the same way. A tortoise lives in our garden and he said it is wiser than us. A doha?
A doha for the tortoise which carries its faith inside its shell in peace and the proud sword which is drawn in the name of Ram or Rahim, though the Lord named by both has never asked for blood.
tortoise, sword, Ram and Rahim
doha: tortoise and sword, Hindu Muslim fight but God is the same
The washerman in our lane washes the clothes of Hindu and Muslim homes alike, and when riots started someone threatened him, though he carries no sword. A doha?
The washerman does not ask the faith of the cloth, and the sword does not know the Lord it is drawn for.
Compose a doha on the sword that is drawn in the name of Ram against Rahim and the washerman who washes the clothes of both faiths clean, showing which of them serves the one Lord better.
washerman, sword, Ram and Rahim
doha: washerman cleans both Hindu and Muslim clothes, swords draw blood over the same god
At school the kids were divided into Hindu and Muslim teams for a game and they started fighting over whose God was stronger. The teacher did not know what to say. Doha for her?
Two roads bend toward the same Beloved; what use is it to fight over the path?
write a doha on how all faiths lead to the same God
many paths, same Lord
Make a doha for people who think their path to the Lord is the only one, when Hindus and Muslims, rich and poor, wise and simple, are all moving along different roads to the same destination.
The needle stitches Hindu and Muslim cloth alike, and the thief steals from both; neither the needle nor the thief asks of Ram or Rahim.
needle, thief, Ram and Rahim

The tailor's needle stitches clothes for Hindu and Muslim customers alike, and the thief steals from both faiths without any distinction, so why do the pious divide a world that sin and sorrow do not divide?
doha: needle and thief, they dont care if you're Hindu or Muslim
The tailor in our lane, a Muslim, stitched my Hindu father's wedding clothes with his needle, and a thief robbed both their shops the same night. They laughed together afterwards. A doha for them?
The yogi bows with folded hands and the faithful bows with open palms, and the Lord receives them both.
yogi, Hindu, Muslim
doha: yogi and fakir sitting together, no religion fight
A wandering yogi sat with a Muslim fakir under the same shade and shared the same bread, and they asked each other nothing about names, for they both knew the Lord is neither Ram's alone nor Rahim's.
A yogi and an old Muslim man share the same bench outside my building every evening and talk for hours without any quarrel. The younger people could learn from them. Doha?
doha about a palace with Muslim style domes and Hindu style carvings, God is the same
The old palace has a courtyard where the Hindu queen prayed in one corner and the Muslim minister prayed in the other, and the king smiled, knowing the same Lord heard them both.
palace, Ram, Rahim
We visited an old palace where the king gave land to both Hindu and Muslim holy men, and the guide said they all lived in peace. A doha on that?
In the old palace both faiths bowed under one roof, and the Lord was not offended.
one Lord, many names
My neighbour's Hindu son and Muslim daughter are best friends, and when someone asked them whose God is real, the girl said, 'Mine and yours are the same.' Can you write a doha?
doha about Allah and Ishwar being the same
Allah, Ishwar, the Name changes with the speaker but not with the Lord.
A doha that tells those who fight over Allah and Ishwar, Ram and Rahim, that the names are only the cloth the Lord wears in each country and each language, and none of them are the Lord himself.
Jaggery is made by a Hindu farmer and eaten by a Muslim child, sweet in the same way to both mouths, as is the love of the Lord who is called Ram by one and Rahim by the other.
doha: jaggery tastes the same to Hindus and Muslims, God's love too
jaggery, Ram, Rahim
Jaggery is sweet to all mouths; the Lord is sweet to all hearts.
During Eid and Diwali, my Hindu and Muslim neighbours exchange jaggery sweets, and everyone says they taste the same. Could you write a doha on that?
A doha on the fire that cooks the Hindu's meal and the Muslim's bread and the pot of water that quenches both their thirsts, showing that Ram and Rahim are served by the same gifts of the world.
doha: fire and pot of water are shared by Hindus and Muslims, God too
In our village the Hindu and Muslim women use the same fire to cook and the same pot of water, but the men fight over their prayers. Doha for the women?
fire, pot of water, Ram
The fire cooks for both, the pot of water quenches both; why should the Lord be shared out in halves?
The Hindu pujari and the Muslim imam in our colony have been arguing about loudspeakers, but on Sundays both of them sit and drink tea together. Doha for them?
Write a doha on Hindu and Muslim neighbours who have shared every sorrow and festival for generations, and now allow slogans to split them, though the Lord named in every slogan is the same.
doha: hindu and muslim neighbours shouldn't fight over religion
neighbours, one Lord
For generations they shared bread; a slogan now divides the table.
doha: lock on the Hindu prayer hall and lock on the Muslim one, God is outside both, with a bier going past
A lock on one prayer hall and a lock on the other, a bier passing both; the Lord has never been locked in.
A doha about the lock on a Hindu prayer hall and the lock on the Muslim one, each guarded against the other, though the Lord who is said to live in both walks free beyond the bier of all.
lock, bier, Ram, Rahim
After the riot, a lock was put on the gates of both prayer halls in our lane, Hindu and Muslim, and the bier of a young man from each side was carried out the same week. A doha for that?
My daughter's school had Diwali and Eid celebrations together, and the children could not tell which God belonged to which festival. A doha?
Two festivals, one joy, one Lord, with different names on the walls and the lips.
Diwali, Eid, one Lord
Say in a doha how the children celebrate Diwali with sweets and Eid with new clothes, and see only joy, while their elders see only differences, though the Lord is the same in every festival.
doha: Diwali and Eid together because God is one
doha: mirror and sword, Hindu and Muslim see the same face and fight
A doha on the mirror in which a Hindu and a Muslim see the same human face, with the same eyes, and the sword that one raises against the other, which cuts the Lord's own image in both.
In the mirror, Hindu and Muslim meet the same face; and yet one lifts a sword.
mirror, sword, Ram and Rahim
In our town's riot, a Hindu man and a Muslim man faced each other with swords in the street, and when one saw himself in a shop mirror, he lowered the weapon. A doha?
My friend's mother is Hindu and father Muslim, and she says that at home she had both an idol and a prayer mat, and all she learned was love. Could you write a doha?
doha: Hindu mother, Muslim father, one family, one God
mixed family, one God
Idol on one wall, prayer mat on the other, and love between them, which is the Lord's own name.
For a child who is raised by a Hindu mother and a Muslim father and learns that each of them prays to the same Beloved by different words, and that love is the only creed worth keeping.

A doha on the pointless quarrels between sects, Hindu against Muslim, Vaishnav against Shaiv, each convinced the others are lost, and how the Lord laughs at all of it because the Lord is neither sect's possession.
doha on how different sects fight but God is one
sectarian fights, fools
Sects quarrel about the shape of the road while the destination smiles.
Our community has split into two groups over which procession route is holier, and both claim that God favours them. My grandmother just laughed and said Ram doesn't care. Doha idea?
I overheard two old men in the lane argue whether Ram is greater than Rahim, then share their tea and agree it didn't matter. A doha?
doha: arguing about Ram vs Rahim, then sharing tea
Ram vs Rahim, silly
A doha for two old friends who quarrelled over which name of the Lord is greater, Ram or Rahim, and then sat down together over tea and realised they had been praising one friend all along.
Over a cup of tea they discovered the One they had been arguing for.
Hindus go to one holy place and Muslims go to another, but the one they seek is not to be found by mere travelling, for he is as near to a Hindu as a Muslim, in the heart of each.
Hindu and Muslim, same God
doha about not needing to go to a holy place to find God, whichever religion you are
Hindus go east, Muslims go west, and the Lord sits quietly at home.
My Hindu aunt goes on pilgrimage each year and my Muslim uncle goes to Mecca, and each calls the other's journey useless. Doha?
A doha about the fire of religious hate that burns Hindu homes and Muslim homes alike, where the flames know no names, and about the Lord who weeps at both and whose name is one in every heart.
The fire does not ask the faith of what it burns; the Lord does not ask the faith of what He loves.
fire, Hindu, Muslim
doha: the fire of religious hatred burns both sides
In last month's riot, a fire burned both a Hindu shop and a Muslim shop on the same street, and the owners cried together over the ruins. A doha?
lock, Ram, Rahim
doha: put a lock on your hate, not on God's name
After the clash in our colony, the Hindu and Muslim boys put a lock on the common playground, and now no child can play. Please write a doha
The lock on the gate of the playground does not lock the Lord out of either heart.
A doha for those who lock their hearts against neighbours of another faith, though the same Lord who is called Ram by one is called Rahim by the other and has no lock He cannot open.
One stream runs through both towns, and its waters do not ask who drinks.
A doha on how the same light rises over the Hindu village and the Muslim village, the same rain falls on both fields, and the same Lord watches over all, yet men build walls between their prayers.
doha: same sky, same rain, same God, why fight over religion
In my hometown, Hindus and Muslims share the same water and the same sky, but people only talk about differences when elections are near. A doha?
one sky, one Lord
It rained a little at dawn, and dew covered the Hindu prayer ground and the Muslim one equally, and salt from the sea air dried on both. A doha on that peace?
Dew falls on both prayer grounds, salt dries on both; the Lord is not on one side.
dew, salt, Ram, Rahim
doha: dew falls on everyone, salt in the wind, same for hindus and muslims, God is one

A doha on the dew that falls equally on the Hindu's prayer ground and the Muslim's, and the salt carried on the same wind, so that nature itself reminds us that the Lord makes no difference between the faiths.
palace, one-string lute, Hindu, Muslim
A wandering singer with a one-string lute is invited to both the Hindu raja's palace and the Muslim nawab's palace in the old stories my grandmother tells. A doha?
The singer with a one-string lute was welcomed in the palace of the Hindu king and the Muslim sultan alike, and sang to both that the Lord is one and the name is only a garment.
doha: palace and a one-string lute, singer for both Hindu and Muslim courts
The one-string lute plays in two palaces, and the song is one.
The elephant carries the Hindu god in procession, the bell rings in the Muslim lane too, and the Lord is carried by neither.
doha: elephant and bell, Hindus and Muslims both celebrate, God is the same
The elephant walks in the Hindu procession and the bell rings from the Muslim neighbourhood too, and everyone who hears them is stirred by the same call, though they say they follow different Gods.
During the procession, an elephant passed a Muslim neighbourhood, and the bell of an ice cream cart rang, and children of both faiths ran to see it. Doha for their joy?
elephant, bell, Ram and Rahim
doha: hindu muslim unity is the answer to riots
After the riots my Muslim colleague and I decided to have lunch together every day to show our children what peace looks like. A doha?
Two lunches, two prayers, and one table where peace is served.
Write a doha about the peace that comes when Hindu and Muslim neighbours share a table after a time of fear, learning once more that the Lord they feared to lose was never divided.
unity, shared table
doha: Muslim and Hindu kids praying side by side in a school
Children fold their hands and open their palms at once, and the Lord gets both gifts.
At my son's school, the Hindu and Muslim children say their prayers in the same room at assembly, and the parents who complain are the ones who forgot how to pray. Could you write a doha?

A doha about a classroom of children, some folding hands in the Hindu way, others raising palms in the Muslim way, each at ease in the presence of the same Lord, while their elders squabble over names.
children, shared prayer
A Muslim friend gave my Hindu mother a leaf of her tulsi plant, and my mother put it near the idol and said that it was God's leaf, whatever name. Doha?
doha: a leaf from a Muslim neighbour in a Hindu puja, God accepts all
A doha about the leaf plucked by a Muslim neighbour and offered in a Hindu ceremony, and how the Lord accepts it with the same grace, since He looks to the heart that gives, not the giver's name.
A leaf from a neighbour's hand is sacred to the Lord, whichever name the giver calls Him.
leaf, Ram, Rahim
doha: bitter gourd is bitter for Hindu and Muslim, so is hatred
Both Hindu and Muslim families in our colony hate bitter gourd and love sweets, and my grandmother says that shows we are all the same people. A doha on that?
The bitter gourd tastes bitter to the Hindu and the Muslim alike, and so does hatred, which makes both faiths suffer, and the Lord named Ram and Rahim is the one remedy.
bitter gourd, Hindu, Muslim
Bitter gourd is bitter to every palate, and love is sweet to every heart.
doha: jaggery at Eid and Diwali, same sweetness, same God
A doha about the sweetness of jaggery shared at Diwali by Hindu homes and at Eid by Muslim ones, so that the same taste fills both festivals, as the same Lord fills both faiths and all names.
jaggery, Hindu and Muslim
During Eid and Diwali, my Hindu and Muslim neighbours exchange jaggery sweets, and the kids cannot say who made which. Can you write a doha?
Sweet jaggery crosses the fence between homes and between faiths.
Two flowers, one fragrance; two prayers, one Lord.
Write a verse for those who build walls between the Hindu place of prayer and the Muslim place of prayer, though the Lord, who needs no walls, is present in the open space between them.
two faiths, one Lord
My grandmother, who lived through Partition, says the Hindu and Muslim families in her old village shared everything and cried together when they parted. Could you write a doha for her memory?
doha about partition and how religion divided people who were the same
doha: how do we stop religious fights? remember God is one
In my WhatsApp group, a Hindu and Muslim friend started sending hateful messages about each other's gods, and I want to send them something wiser. A doha?
A doha that asks every Hindu and every Muslim to put down their anger and listen to the quiet in their own hearts, where the Lord has only one voice and says the same thing to both.
Put down the quarrel, take up the Name, and find that the Name is the same.
stop the religious fight
A thief broke into a Hindu holy place and a Muslim prayer hall in our town the same night, and he didn't care about either faith. The sandalwood of the idol and a prayer cap were both stolen. Doha?
doha: thief steals from both Hindu and Muslim holy places, sandalwood too, no religion
thief, sandalwood, both faiths
The thief took sandalwood from one and silver from the other, and neither God complained, for the thief had one hunger and they had one Lord.

A doha on the thief who robbed both the Hindu holy place and the Muslim prayer hall, sandalwood from one and carpet from the other, for he saw no difference between them, though the pious saw only difference.
heron, Hindu, Muslim
The heron stands in the pond at the edge of the Hindu village and the Muslim village alike, patient and still, and shows both faiths how to wait in silence for the same Lord.
Near our town there is a pond where the Hindu and Muslim boys play together in the evenings, and a heron watches them like an elder. A doha?
The heron stands at the water's edge, in silence, whichever village claims the pond.
doha: the heron in the pond is more peaceful than Hindus and Muslims
Under the same tree the one-string lute sang, and the Hindu and the Muslim sat together to hear the song of the One.

A doha about a wandering singer who plays his one-string lute under a tree where Hindus and Muslims sit together to listen, with no thought of faith, because the song needs no name to touch the heart.
doha: one-string lute under a tree, Hindus and Muslims listening together
In the evenings an old man sings under a tree in our park with a one-string lute, and Hindu and Muslim families gather without a word about their faiths. A doha?
one-string lute, tree, Ram
A doha on the skeleton in the desert sand which no one can call Hindu or Muslim, because death has stripped away every name, and what remains is only what the Lord made, which is the same in all.
skeleton, sand, Hindu, Muslim
Sand fills the skull of a skeleton; no one can tell whose God he called.
In the desert sand we found a skeleton, and our guide said he could have been from any faith. I couldn't stop thinking about it. A doha?
doha: skeleton in the sand has no religion
Whether it is the temple's morning chant or the call of the Muslim crier at dawn, the sound goes up to the same Lord, and those who quarrel about which is nearer are deaf to both. A doha?
doha: temple and prayer hall are both just roads to the same Lord
Our town has a temple next to a prayer hall, and for years the two communities shared the same lane, until recently when slogans began. Could you write a doha?
The temple and the prayer hall point to the same sky.
temple, prayer hall, one Lord
shared faith, shared city
doha: the city belongs to both Hindus and Muslims, so does God
Write a doha on how the old city was built by Hindu masons and Muslim architects, with domes and spires side by side, so that its beauty is the beauty of both faiths together, and so is the Lord.
Dome and spire stand side by side, and the sky welcomes both.
I grew up in an old city where a Hindu mason and a Muslim carpenter built our family home together, and neither of them ever argued about whose God was better. A doha?
snake, Ram, Rahim
A doha about the snake that bites a Hindu and a Muslim alike, whose venom knows no faith, and the antidote of love, which is the same for both, because the Lord who heals is one.
The snake does not ask the faith it bites; the cure does not ask the faith it heals.
doha: snake bite doesn't care if you're Hindu or Muslim, why should we
A snake bit a boy in our village, and both a Hindu and a Muslim doctor rushed to help, and nobody asked whose faith he followed. A doha for this?
doha: tongue and touchstone, a test of truth, both Hindu and Muslim have the same test

The speaker says Ram or Rahim according to habit, but the touchstone of the heart tests only love, and finds the devotion is the same in Hindu and Muslim alike. A doha on the tongue and the touchstone.
tongue, touchstone, Ram and Rahim
The touchstone tests the heart, not the tongue; there the Hindu and the Muslim are weighed the same.
My grandmother says she can tell a real believer not by what their tongue says, Hindu or Muslim, but by how they behave, like testing on a touchstone. Doha?
doha: Eid and Holi at the same time this year, God is happy
This year Eid and Holi came within the same week and our colony celebrated both together with no fights. A doha on that?
Eid, Holi, joy
Write a doha about the colours of Holi and the greetings of Eid mixing in one street, the children's faces coloured and the elders embracing, as if the Lord had arranged the two festivals to meet.
Colours of Holi, embraces of Eid; the Lord mixes them in the same lane.
A cloth sheet is spread under both faiths in their hour of rest, and the Lord watches over the sleepers.
A doha about a cloth sheet the Hindu mother spreads for the Muslim guest and the Muslim mother spreads for the Hindu, a shared hospitality that proves the Lord is the same in both homes.
cloth sheet, Hindu, Muslim
doha: cloth sheet given to a stranger of another faith, kindness is one religion
When the flood came, a Hindu family gave a cloth sheet to a Muslim family sleeping on the road, and that was all that was said. Doha for their kindness?
yogi, tree, Ram, Rahim
Under the tree the yogi and the maulvi sit; the shade does not ask whose God they praise.
doha: yogi and Muslim man under the same tree, same God
There is an old tree in our village where a yogi and an elderly Muslim man play chess every afternoon, and neither mentions religion. Could you write a doha about them?
A doha about a yogi and a Muslim saint who sit beneath the same tree and speak of love for the Lord, one calling him Ram and the other Rahim, and the tree giving the same shade to both.
Please write a doha about the fakir who walks the roads owning nothing at all and so has nothing that a tax collector or a king could ever take from him, and sleeps without any fear.
My college friend left a salaried job to live on almost nothing, and I have never seen anyone so unafraid of tomorrow.
Who owns nothing fears nothing; the king trembles on his seat while the fakir laughs at the wind.
doha about the freedom of having nothing to lose
owning nothing, fearing nothing
I want a doha about a wandering holy man who gave up every possession on purpose, who is richer in freedom than the wealthy, and who walks into any town without worry about what could be lost.
When burglars hit our street, the only home they left alone belonged to the old fakir who had nothing and sat on his step smiling.
fakir's freedom
Naked of possessions, light of heart, the fakir goes where he pleases, for nothing holds him back.
write a doha on giving up everything to be free
doha about a fakir who sees himself in a mirror and sees someone who owns nothing and fears nothing
mirror, fakir, fearless
The fakir looks into the mirror and sees only a face without need, and a heart without fear.
My uncle gave away his mirror, his watch, and his shiny things last year, and says he finally looks at himself without worry.
Write a doha where a fakir looks into a mirror and finds nothing to hide, nothing to polish, nothing to lose, and declares himself the freest of men because he chose to own nothing.
My cousin burned through his savings chasing a get-rich scheme, and my aunt who owns nothing just laughed and said, the philosopher's stone is owning nothing and fearing nothing.
doha with philosopher's stone, how the wandering saint with nothing is richer than a rich man
philosopher's stone, owning nothing

Please write a doha where the fakir refuses the philosopher's stone that could turn all to wealth, because he knows that owning nothing brings a freedom no wealth can match, and a fear that no robber can arouse.
The philosopher's stone is offered to the fakir, and he smiles, for he who owns nothing has already found the greater treasure.
potter, clay, rainbird, nothing owned
The potter in our lane gave his whole shop to his son, took nothing but his clay-stained clothes, and now sits happily listening for the rainbird.
Write a doha about a fakir who owns neither clay nor wheel nor the potter's trade, who listens for the rainbird and sleeps wherever evening finds him, free because there is nothing left to lose.
The potter's clay is broken and forgotten, the rainbird calls, and the fakir who owns nothing is afraid of nothing.
doha with a potter and clay and a rainbird, about the freedom of owning nothing
Light is the one who has set down every burden, and the road welcomes him like a friend.
doha about choosing to live with nothing and being totally fearless

Please write a doha for someone who has given away everything they owned of their own free will and discovered that having nothing means there is nothing to protect, nothing to fear and nothing to lose.
After I sold everything and moved into a rented room with a single bag, I slept better than I had in ten years.
nothing owned, nothing feared
In my uncle's village, every home has a heavy lock except the fakir's hut, which stands open, and he has never once been robbed or afraid.
doha with a lock, about a fakir who needs no lock because he owns nothing
lock, nothing to guard
No lock hangs on the fakir's hut, for what is there to keep, and what is there to fear?
Write a doha where the rich man fits a heavy lock to guard his goods while the fakir has nothing to lock away, so that the poor man alone sleeps in freedom and without worry.
fish, fakir's freedom
A fish in the water owns nothing, carries nothing, and fears no robber, and the fakir who has chosen to own nothing lives the same carefree life; please write a doha on that.
doha with a fish, about a fakir who owns nothing and has no fear
The fish owns no pond, the fakir owns no roof, and both drift free wherever life takes them.
Watching a fish dart through the shallows I thought of my friend who gave up his home and job and now travels freely with a single bag.
furnace, fakir, fearless
The furnace roars for the rich man's gain, while the fakir warms himself with his own freedom and fears no ending.
Write a doha where a furnace burns day and night for a merchant counting his profits, and a fakir passes by with empty hands, free from every worry that profit brings to the owner.
doha with a furnace, about the fakir who owns nothing and so fears nothing
The owner of the foundry down the road works the furnace around the clock to protect his business, while a wandering holy man sleeps soundly outside his gate.
He who has thrown away his bundle of wants walks on, singing, with all the sky for his roof.

I'd like a doha that celebrates the person who chose to live with nothing, who has no savings to lose, no property to defend, and no reputation to guard, and who therefore walks through the world without a tremble.
owning nothing, free
doha on a fakir who gave up everything and is happy
My neighbour gave away his flat, his car and his bank account, and when I asked if he was afraid, he said there was nothing left to be afraid for.
The touchstone tests the wares of the merchant and finds some of it false, but it cannot test the fakir, who owns nothing and so has nothing that could be found wanting. Please write a doha on that.
When the banker's investments were tested by the crash, he lost sleep for weeks, and the wandering saint at his gate, who owned nothing, was not troubled at all.
The touchstone can test the trader's treasure, but what can it test in the fakir, who carries nothing and fears nothing?
doha with a touchstone, about the fakir who owns nothing
touchstone, nothing to test
Poor in possessions, rich in being, the fakir walks the world as a king walks his garden.
choosing to own nothing

Please write a doha about the quiet pride of the one who chose to be without, who needs no one's permission, fears no one's anger and lacks no one's approval, because there is nothing anyone can take.
doha on the freedom of the mendicant who owns nothing
My grandmother gave her last ornaments to the shrine and then said, now I can finally go anywhere without worry.
When we were robbed on a train, the saintly old man in our compartment, who carried only a cloth bag, was the one who sat completely calm; I want a doha on him.
Please compose a doha about a wandering faqir who has nothing to be robbed of, nothing to be proud of and nothing to be afraid of, and who therefore feels richer than a rich man travelling in fear.
The robber leaves the fakir untouched, for what does he have to steal from one who has chosen to have nothing?
fakir, empty-handed, fearless
doha on how having nothing means no fear
A rope binds the cattle of the rich man, the buckets of the village, the chests of the merchant, and the fakir owns no rope because he is bound to nothing. Write a doha about his freedom.
Our village headman is tied by a hundred ropes of obligation to his land, while the wandering fakir who passes through each winter is tied to nothing and smiles at everything.
Every rope of ownership ties a man to the earth, and the fakir has cut them all and walks as light as air.
rope, unbound fakir
doha with a rope, about a fakir who owns nothing so nothing ties him down
The salt of the sea is the weaver's wage, yet the fakir wants neither salt nor cloth, and that is his wealth.
salt, loom, owning nothing
doha with salt and a weaver's loom, a fakir who gave up everything
Write a doha where a weaver at his loom works for a pinch of salt and a day's cloth, while a fakir who has chosen to own neither passes by, freer than both the weaver and the trader.
My friend sold his loom and his small salt business to wander on the road, saying he would rather own nothing and fear nothing.
The fakir rests a night at the inn with a small lamp, and by morning he has left without a single thing behind.
Please write a doha about a fakir who stays a night at an inn, has no possessions to unpack, lights a little lamp for company, and leaves at dawn with nothing lost, as free and fearless as ever.
At a small inn on my trip, the only guest who slept deeply was the old fakir by the lamp, who had nothing to guard and nothing to pack.
doha with an inn and a lamp, about a fakir who owns nothing
inn, lamp, nothing owned
doha with fire and a moneylender, about a fakir who owns nothing and fears nothing
When fire consumes the moneylender's ledgers he weeps for his loss, but the fakir sits calmly by the same fire, because he has no records of debt and no hoard to lose. Please write a doha for that.
fire, moneylender, fakir
After the fire at the money-lender's office everyone ran to save what they could, and the old fakir across the road just sat and watched, completely at ease.
Fire takes the moneylender's ledger and the fakir's silence alike, but only the fakir smiles.
I have been living with just two sets of clothes for a year now, and I have never felt more free from worry.
What the fakir has not gathered, the world cannot steal, and what the fakir has not loved of the world, the world cannot take.
Please write a doha for a person who has decided to let go of most of their belongings, finds that they are more at ease, and sees that owning nothing is a kind of strength that no loss can touch.
fearless poverty chosen
doha about the fakir who has nothing to fear
The wheel is idle, the bridge is crossed, and the fakir walks on with nothing, for owning nothing weighs nothing.
My aunt gave away her spinning wheel and her small plot, crossed the bridge to the ashram, and told us she had never felt so light.
spinning wheel, bridge, fakir
doha with a spinning wheel and a bridge, about a fakir with nothing to lose
Write a doha where the fakir leaves his spinning wheel at the bank, crosses the bridge with empty hands, and walks into the town with no fear, because he has nothing that anyone could take from him.

I want a doha about the rare joy of the person who chose to live with almost nothing, who sleeps wherever he is, eats whatever he is given and fears neither theft nor loss nor the opinions of the rich.
doha for the free spirit who owns nothing
fakir, utterly free
A poor man's cloak with a king's heart: this is the fakir, owning nothing, fearing nothing, answerable to none.
A man at my gym quit his job, sold his flat, and now lives out of one small bag, and he has the calmest face I have seen.
The mountain asks nothing of the tree and the tree owns nothing of the mountain, and the fakir sits between, as free as both.
Write a doha where a fakir sits beneath a tree on a mountain, owning neither tree nor mountain nor so much as a blanket, and finds that this very absence of ownership frees him from every fear.
On our trek up the mountain we passed an old man sleeping under a tree with nothing but a cloth bag, and he looked like the freest soul alive.
doha with a mountain and a tree, about a fakir who owns nothing
mountain, tree, owning nothing
moon, fakir, fearless
The moon keeps no estate and counts no savings, and the fakir who sleeps beneath it with nothing to call his own shares in her freedom; please write a doha about this joy of owning nothing.
doha with the moon, about a fakir who has nothing to lose
One night I saw a homeless-looking holy man sleeping on the roadside under the full moon with the calmest face, and I envied him.
The moon is the fakir's companion and the fakir the moon's guest, and neither owns a single thing.
crossroads, fakir, free
At the crossroads the fakir stands with empty hands, for every road is his and none of them is owned.
Write a doha where a fakir reaches a crossroads and need not decide which road to take for gain, because he owns nothing and fears nothing, and every path is open to the free.
doha with a crossroads, about a fakir who owns nothing so he can go anywhere
I stood at a crossroads of my own life last year and gave up my job to do what I love, with almost no money, and for the first time I felt unafraid.

Please write a doha about a person who gave away the family property and now lives in a rented corner, owning nothing and wanting nothing, and who is happier than any of the relatives who quarrelled over the land.
chosen emptiness, fearless
Having nothing, the fakir has everything, for there is nothing between him and the open sky.
doha about giving away everything and being free
When my father signed the family land over to the village school he looked ten years younger.
The village physician, who earns almost nothing, once said the only man he could not worry about was the old fakir who rowed his boat across each morning with nothing to his name.
Write a doha where a physician and a fakir share a boat across the water, and the physician carries medicines and fears for them while the fakir owns nothing and fears nothing, free as the wind.
doha with a boat and a physician, about a fakir with nothing to lose
boat, physician, fakir
The physician guards his herbs in the boat, the fakir guards nothing, and the fakir alone crosses without fear.
bitter gourd, cleric, fakir
The cleric wears his garb of learning, the fakir only his freedom; one feasts, the other eats bitter gourd and is not afraid.
doha with a bitter gourd and a cleric, about a fakir who owns nothing
Write a doha where a cleric argues over property and rank while a fakir eats a plain bitter gourd under the open sky, owning nothing and fearing nothing, and is the happier of the two.
At the wedding the cleric argued about the fees, while the fakir at the entrance, who had nothing and asked for nothing, ate his bitter gourd curry quietly and left.
The heron stands on a stone with nothing and fears no hunter, and the fakir sits beside it, owning nothing, as free as the bird.
Walking along the lake I saw a heron on a stone, and an old mendicant sitting beside it with no bag at all, both of them equally unbothered.
doha with a heron and a stone, about a fakir with nothing to lose
stone, heron, owning nothing

Write a doha where a fakir sits on a stone beside a patient heron, both of them owning nothing and wanting nothing, and neither is troubled by any fear, since neither has anything that could be taken.
doha about how having nothing means youre totally free
nothing to lose
The fakir has locked nothing and counted nothing, and for that reason he alone is at ease in the world.
Please write a doha for the one who chooses to live without owning anything, finds that he has no fear of loss, and walks through the world as a guest who has already paid his debts.
A friend who sold his belongings and left on a long pilgrimage with just a backpack wrote that he has never been so unafraid of anything in his life.
churn, clay, fakir
My grandmother's churn and the potter's clay are the only things she kept when she gave everything else away, and she says she has never been so free from worry.
The churn is empty, the clay is dry, and the fakir who needs neither sleeps free of every fear.
doha with a churn and potter and clay, about a fakir with nothing
Write a doha where a fakir passes a woman at her churn and a potter at his clay, both of whom work to own more, and he blesses them, owning nothing, fearing nothing, and walks on.
Beside the oil press and the cremation ground the fakir sleeps with nothing, for the ground takes all alike and he has already given his all.
doha with an oil press and a cremation ground, about a fakir who owns nothing
Our colony fakir sleeps near the oil press and the cremation ground, owning nothing, and he is the only person I know who is not afraid of either.

Write a doha where a fakir sits between the oil press and the cremation ground, one grinding for gain and the other claiming all, and he alone is calm because he already owns nothing for either to take.
oil press, cremation ground, fakir
The boat carries the fakir across the water and he has nothing but a shroud's worth of cloth, and no fear of the far shore.
Aboard the ferry, the only passenger without luggage was an old man in a plain wrap that looked almost like a shroud, and he sat with perfect calm.

Write a doha where a fakir crosses water in a boat wearing something like a shroud, owning nothing more, and fearing neither storm nor shore, since he has already given up everything the water could take.
boat, shroud, fakir
doha with a boat and a shroud, about a fakir who owns nothing
Please write a doha about the fakir who is offered a bar of gold by a rich patron and gently refuses, saying that a man who owns nothing walks lighter than a man weighed down by even a little.
doha with gold, about a fakir who says no to riches
Someone once tried to give my uncle a gold chain for his kindness, and he returned it, saying a man with nothing is a man with no fear.
Gold shines before the fakir's eyes and he turns away, for he knows what the owner never learns: what is owned, owns.
gold refused, fearless
The old woman who sells swans of clay in our village eats only bitter gourd and rice, owns nothing beyond her room, and walks about with the calm of someone who has no fear at all.
doha with bitter gourd and a swan, about a fakir who has nothing
bitter gourd, swan, fakir
The swan owns the whole lake without a deed, the fakir eats bitter gourd without a care, and both are rich in being free.
Write a doha where a fakir shares his simple meal of bitter gourd beside a swan on the lake, owning nothing, fearing nothing, and finding that his emptiness is the greatest freedom a person can have.
A shroud has no pockets and a tree has no deed, and the fakir who knows this lives under the tree as if already in a shroud, owning nothing and fearing nothing. Please write a doha for this.
shroud, tree, fakir
Under the tree the fakir lies in his plain shroud-like cloth, and the world's keepers of property cannot reach him.
doha with a shroud and a tree, about the fakir who owns nothing
I met a quiet old man under a tree who had given everything away and now wore only a plain white wrap, and he told me he is afraid of nothing.
My teacher gave away his books, his home and his salary, and now moves from town to town, free as the wind, unafraid of what tomorrow will bring.
The fakir has nothing to shut, no seat to lose, no name to protect; he is what remains when nothing is held.
nothing owned, nothing feared
Please write a doha about the dignity of a person who chose to be without, whose freedom comes from having nothing to defend, and who is unafraid of what the world can do to him.
write a doha on the freedom of the wandering saint who owns nothing
The washerman scrubs the rich man's cloth, the chakor bird watches the night sky, and the fakir owns neither and is happier than both.
washerman, chakor bird, fakir
doha with a washerman and a chakor bird, about a fakir who owns nothing
Write a doha where a washerman works for a few coins and a chakor bird gazes at the sky with longing, while a fakir who owns nothing passes by free, fearless and contented in his emptiness.
A washerman in our lane told me that the fakir sleeping near his ghat is the only person in town who does not worry about money.

I would like a doha for those who have chosen to live without possessions, who find that nothing owned means nothing feared, and who walk through life with a peace the owners of the world can only envy.
free because empty-handed
With nothing in his hands, the fakir holds the whole world lightly; with nothing to lose, he cannot lose.
doha about the fakir who chose to own nothing
At my friend's minimalist home everything is gone except a mat and a cup, and she says she has never been so unafraid.
The rich man keeps a bird in a cage and fears for his home, while a fakir sleeps in the mosque courtyard owning nothing, caged by nothing, and afraid of nothing; please write a doha on the contrast.
The cage holds the bird, the mosque holds the prayer, and the fakir, who owns nothing, is held by no one.
doha with a mosque and a cage, about a fakir who owns nothing and is free
Outside the mosque a man sleeps on the steps with nothing and no fear, while the trader nearby keeps a hundred worries.
mosque, cage, fakir
ocean, fakir, fearless
At the beach I met an elderly man with no belongings who stared at the ocean without any concern at all and said, I own the same ocean you do.

Write a doha where a fakir stands before the ocean, owning nothing, wanting nothing, and fearing no wave, because a man who has given up all possession has nothing left that the ocean could ever take.
The ocean takes the rich man's ship and the fakir's silence is never touched, for he has nothing to lose to it.
doha with the ocean, about a fakir who has nothing and fears nothing
sword, snake, fakir
Our neighbour who guards his goods with a sword by the bed jumps at every sound, while the wandering fakir who sleeps outside, even near snakes, rests as calm as a baby.
The sword is for the owner and the snake for the careless, but the fakir owns nothing and is bitten by neither fear.
Write a doha where a fakir lies down beside a snake and a sword left by the road, owning nothing and fearing nothing, while those who own much tremble at every hint of loss.
doha with a sword and a snake, about the fakir who has nothing to fear
A drop of dew on the fakir's hand is all he owns, and it is more than enough to keep him free.
doha with dew, about a fakir who owns nothing, not even a bowl
I woke early at the monastery, saw the monk walking barefoot through the dew with no belongings, and felt a calm I'd never known.
Please write a doha where a fakir walks barefoot through the morning dew with empty hands, carrying nothing and fearing nothing, as light as the dew itself, and shows what it is to be free of owning.
dew, owning nothing
nothing lost, nothing feared
When my business collapsed I was devastated, but my grandmother, who gave up her holdings years ago, said she had never missed any of it and she looked at me with such peace.
doha for the fakir who owns nothing and so is free
To own nothing is to be owned by nothing, and to fear nothing is to be king of everything.

Please write a doha for the person who has realised that every possession is a worry, every title a fear, and who therefore chose to walk lightly, owning nothing, in a freedom no wealthy man has ever known.
On the old ferry boat the only passenger with no luggage was a thin fakir who sat beside a tortoise someone had caught, and he looked calmer than the wealthy merchants around him.
boat, tortoise, fakir
Write a doha where a fakir rides in a boat with a tortoise that carries its entire home on its back, while he carries nothing at all, owning nothing and free from every fear of loss.
The tortoise carries its home and the boat carries its load, but the fakir carries nothing and sails like the wind.
doha with a boat and a tortoise, about a fakir who owns nothing
doha with a chakor bird and a palace, about the fakir who owns nothing
chakor bird, palace, fakir
Outside the palace gates a chakor bird sang while a wandering saint who owned nothing walked right through the crowd without fear.
The palace owns a thousand rooms and the chakor owns its longing for the sky, but the fakir owns nothing, and no one can threaten him.
Write a doha where a fakir walks through the gates of a great palace, while a chakor bird looks on, and the fakir, owning nothing, fears no guard, no king, and no loss, and is the freest soul there.
doha with philosopher's stone and a needle, about the fakir who owns nothing
philosopher's stone, needle, fakir
A friend of mine hunted for an investment that would turn everything into riches, while his grandmother, who owns one needle and one cloth, laughed at him for fearing loss.

Write a doha where the fakir is offered a philosopher's stone and a needle of silver but declines both, saying that owning nothing frees him from every fear of loss, and that this is the greatest alchemy.
Let the philosopher's stone be turned to wealth, the fakir needs only a needle to mend his single cloth.
Write a doha where a yogi in a cotton wrap sits with his hands empty, owning nothing but the breath he breathes, and finds that this very poverty is the greatest freedom a man can know.
Cotton on the body and nothing in the hand, the yogi sits fearless, for there is no one who can take from him.
